questions.q: On which port does the Connect REST API listen when `listeners` is not set?

options.why: 9092 is the broker's default listener port.
8081 isn't Connect's default; with no listeners set, the REST API uses 8083.
That's the controller listener in Kafka's sample config.

questions.explain: Without `listeners`, the Connect REST server runs on port 8083 over HTTP, in both standalone and distributed mode.

questions.q: Which request creates a new connector?

options.t: POST /connectors, with a name and a config
PUT /connectors/{name}/start with the config in the body
options.why: There is no start endpoint; connectors start when created.
That path lists or validates plugins.

questions.explain: `POST /connectors` creates a connector; the body has a `name` and a `config` object, and optionally `initial_state`.

questions.q: Which request shows whether a connector and each of its tasks are running or failed, and on which worker?
questions.explain: `GET /connectors/{name}/status` returns the connector's state, its worker, error information if it failed, and the state of all its tasks.

questions.q: A source system is down for maintenance for two hours. The team wants the connector to stop polling but resume quickly afterwards. Which request fits best?

options.why: Deleting removes the connector and its configuration.
Stop frees resources, so starting again takes longer.

questions.explain: Pause stops message processing but leaves the tasks' resources allocated, so it resumes quickly. Stop shuts tasks down and frees resources, saving them but taking longer to start again.

questions.q: A team must reset a source connector's offsets through the REST API. What state must the connector be in first?

options.why: Offsets can be changed only when the connector is stopped.

options.t: RUNNING, so the change takes effect at once
options.why: A running connector's offsets can't be changed.

questions.explain: `DELETE` and `PATCH /connectors/{name}/offsets` need the connector to exist and be stopped (`PUT /connectors/{name}/stop`).

questions.q: Which request restarts a connector together with only those of its tasks that have failed?

options.why: Resume restarts processing of a paused or stopped connector, not failed tasks.

options.t: DELETE then POST the connector again
options.why: That recreates it, losing its state and history.
Patching config doesn't restart failed tasks on its own.

questions.explain: `POST /connectors/{name}/restart` takes `includeTasks` and `onlyFailed`; a single task can also be restarted with `POST /connectors/{name}/tasks/{id}/restart`.

questions.q: A sink task fails with an exception at 02:00. At 09:00 it is still FAILED. Why didn't Connect restart it?

options.t: Connect retries failed tasks automatically, but only once an hour
options.why: Connect doesn't restart failed tasks at all.

options.t: Connect does not restart failed tasks automatically
The worker must be restarted first
options.why: The REST API restarts tasks without a worker restart.

options.t: Failed tasks restart only after a rebalance
options.why: Restarting is a manual action through the REST API.

questions.explain: Connect does not automatically restart failed tasks; use the restart endpoints (a restart during a rebalance returns 409 Conflict).

questions.q: A restart request for a task returns HTTP 409. What does it mean?

options.why: The docs give 409 for a restart attempted during a rebalance.

options.t: The worker that owns the task has run out of heap memory
A rebalance is in progress; retry after it completes

questions.explain: Restarting a task while a rebalance is taking place returns 409 (Conflict). You can retry afterwards, though a rebalance effectively restarts connectors and tasks anyway.

questions.q: Which TWO are valid states for a connector in the status API?
questions.explain: Connector and task states are UNASSIGNED, RUNNING, PAUSED, FAILED and RESTARTING; STOPPED applies to connectors only.

questions.q: A connector is paused and then the whole Connect cluster restarts. What state is the connector in afterwards?

options.t: RUNNING, because a restart clears the pause
UNASSIGNED until someone reassigns it by hand
Still PAUSED, until it is resumed

questions.explain: The pause state is persistent: even after the cluster restarts, the connector won't process messages until it is resumed.

questions.q: A Connect worker crashes. With default settings, when are its tasks given to the other workers?

options.t: Only if it hasn't returned within 5 minutes
Immediately, in a full eager rebalance of every task
options.why: Since 2.3 rebalancing is incremental and delayed for departed workers.

options.t: Never; the tasks wait for the worker to return
options.why: They are reassigned after the delay.

options.t: After the session timeout of 45 seconds

questions.explain: Connect waits `scheduled.rebalance.max.delay.ms` (default 5 minutes) for a departed worker; if it returns it gets its tasks back, otherwise they are reassigned.

questions.q: A new connector is added to a Connect cluster running dozens of tasks. With the default protocol, what happens to the existing tasks?

options.t: All of them stop and restart, as they do in every rebalance
options.why: That was the eager protocol before 2.3.

options.t: They are paused until the new connector is running
Only tasks that must move are stopped and restarted
Nothing; adding a connector never rebalances
options.why: Adding a connector triggers a rebalance.

questions.explain: Since 2.3, Connect uses incremental cooperative rebalancing: only new, removed or moving tasks are affected; others keep running.

questions.q: A worker can't find a connector class that the team installed as a JAR. Which worker setting tells Connect where plugins are?

options.why: That names the class to use; it doesn't say where to find it.

questions.explain: `plugin.path` lists the directories that contain Connect plugins: connectors, converters and transformations.

questions.q: A sink connector must read every topic whose name starts with `orders-`. Which setting fits?

options.why: topics takes a comma-separated list, not a pattern.

questions.explain: Sink connectors take `topics` (a comma-separated list) or `topics.regex` (a Java regular expression).

questions.q: An operator wants to remove one key from a running connector's configuration, leaving the rest as it is. Which request does that?

options.t: PUT /connectors/{name}/config with only that key, set to null
options.why: PUT replaces the whole configuration, so every other key would be lost.

options.t: PATCH /connectors/{name}/config with that key set to null

questions.explain: `PATCH /connectors/{name}/config` patches the configuration; a null value in the body removes that key.

questions.q: Before creating a connector, a team wants to check its configuration and get error messages for bad values. Which endpoint does that?

options.why: That lists topics a connector has used.

questions.explain: `PUT /connector-plugins/{type}/config/validate` validates config values against the plugin's definition, returning suggestions and error messages.

questions.q: What does a change data capture (CDC) source connector deliver into Kafka?

options.t: A nightly full copy of each table
options.why: CDC streams changes as they happen, not periodic copies.

options.t: The database's query logs, as one record for each SQL statement run
options.why: CDC records row changes, not queries.

options.t: The rows inserted, updated and deleted, as change events
Only the schema of each table

questions.explain: CDC records represent which row in a table was inserted, updated or deleted; read in Kafka Streams they form a changelog (a KTable). CDC connectors may also use extra topics, for example for schema history.

questions.q: Which part of Apache Kafka is built on Kafka Connect source connectors?

options.why: Streams is a client library, not Connect-based.
The controller is part of the server.
That's a command-line tool on the producer API.

questions.explain: MirrorMaker 2, which replicates topics, configs, consumer offsets and ACLs between clusters, is built on Kafka Connect source connectors.

questions.q: A team submits a second connector with the same `name` as an existing one. What happens?

options.t: It replaces the first connector's config
Connect appends -2 to the new name

questions.explain: `name` must be unique; attempting to register again with the same name fails (use the config endpoints to change an existing connector).

questions.q: Which TWO statements about pausing versus stopping a connector are right?

options.t: Stopping frees the tasks' resources; pausing keeps them
Only stopping is persistent across cluster restarts
A paused connector resumes faster than a stopped one
A stopped connector keeps polling but discards records

questions.explain: Pause stops processing but leaves resources allocated, so it resumes quickly; stop shuts tasks down and frees resources, so resuming takes longer.

questions.q: How can `connector.class` name the built-in file sink connector?

options.t: Only by its full class name
By full class name, or an alias such as FileStreamSink

options.why: connector.class takes a class name or alias.

questions.explain: `connector.class` accepts the full class name or an alias: `FileStreamSink` or `FileStreamSinkConnector` for `org.apache.kafka.connect.file.FileStreamSinkConnector`.

questions.q: When does standalone mode suit a Connect job best?

options.t: When the job must keep running even when one of its workers fails
When many workers must share a heavy load
options.why: Sharing load across workers is distributed mode.

options.t: When connectors must be created through the REST API
options.why: Both modes have the REST API.

options.t: For a single-worker job, such as collecting log files

questions.explain: Standalone runs one process: simpler, suited to a single-worker job such as collecting log files, but with no fault tolerance.
